artworks.title: Liriope Bringing Narcissus before Tiresias
artworks.description: Carpioni’s Kunsthistorisches Museum canvas (GG 1646) shows the naiad Liriope presenting infant Narcissus to blind Tiresias — Ovid’s opening of the Echo myth. Venetian color keeps the mother visible as the figure who asks the fatal question: will the boy live long if he never knows himself?

artworks.title: Liriope Bringing Narcissus before Tiresias
artworks.description: A second Carpioni treatment of the same Metamorphoses III consultation: Liriope, the river-nymph mother, and the prophet who answers with a riddle. Together the canvases form the rare early-modern gallery that names Liriope rather than only her self-doomed son.

artworks.title: Liriope and Narcissus
artworks.description: Cobaert’s relief pair binds mother and son in one sculptural breath — Liriope as the naiad who bore Narcissus to Cephissus. The work belongs to the Ovidian decorative tradition that kept the nymph’s name alive beside the boy at the pool.

popCulture.title: Metamorphoses III (Narcissus)
popCulture.creator: Ovid
popCulture.description: Ovid opens Narcissus with Liriope’s visit to Tiresias — the Latin passage that made the naiad mother a named hinge of the echo-and-mirror myth.
